notes.title: -(으)ㄹ래?
notes.text: -(으)ㄹ래(요)? is a friendly "want to…?": 커피 마실래? (Want some coffee?) 같이 갈래요? (Want to come along?) Answering with -(으)ㄹ래 says what you'd like: 나는 집에 있을래 (I think I'll stay home). Use it with friends and equals, not your boss.

lessons.goal: Say "in case…" or "worried that…" with -(으)ㄹ까 봐.

notes.title: Restaurant manners
notes.text: Call the staff with 저기요! or 여기요! (Excuse me!) — you don't wait to be noticed. To order: 이거 주세요 (This one, please) or …(으)로 할게요 (I'll have …). There's no tipping in Korea.

notes.title: -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다
notes.text: -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 means "almost… (but didn't)": 넘어질 뻔했어요 (I almost fell). It's always past tense, and usually about something that luckily — or sadly — didn't happen. A favorite exclamation: 큰일 날 뻔했다! (That was a close call!)

notes.title: Drinking etiquette
notes.text: When an older person pours for you, hold your glass with both hands, and turn your head slightly away from elders as you drink. Don't pour your own glass — pour for others and they'll pour for you. Soju always comes with 안주, food to go with drinks. And it's always fine to say 저는 술을 못 마셔요.

notes.title: 장가가다, 시집가다
notes.text: The traditional words for getting married: a man 장가가다 and a woman 시집가다 (literally "goes to the in-laws' house"). Today everyone just says 결혼하다. 미팅 is a group blind date popular with college students; 소개팅 is a one-on-one blind date set up by friends.
